uncited: This method approximates the multiple scattering integral in volumetric shadowing by decomposing the view-independent part of the integrand using Singular Value Decomposition (SVD) in epipolar coordinates.

It solves the problem of high computational cost in per-pixel integration by reducing the complexity from per-pixel to per-slice, allowing for massive parallelism by processing each camera ray independently rather than maintaining interdependent partial sum trees across rays.
It builds on [Variation Along and Across Light Rays (SVD Approximation)](6391-variation-along-and-across-light-rays-svd-approximation.md).
- Light depth map (rectified into epipolar coordinates, stored as shadow map $S$).
- Volume density $\sigma_t$, scattering coefficient $\sigma_s$, phase function $\rho$, and incoming light $L_{\text{in}}$.
- Number of singular vectors $N$ (typically 4).
- Radiance $L(\alpha, \beta)$ for each camera pixel $(\alpha, \beta)$.
- **Rectified Shadow Map $S$**: A 2D array where $S[\alpha, \gamma]$ stores the $\beta$ coordinate (height) of the camera ray at which the light ray $(\alpha, \gamma)$ is blocked.
- These are precomputed once per frame on the CPU.
- **Prefix Sum Tables**: For each singular vector $i \in [1, N]$, a 1D prefix sum table of $\Gamma_i(\gamma) \Delta \gamma$ is computed.
**Change of Variables**: Rewrite the scattering integral in epipolar coordinates $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$.
where $D(\alpha, \beta)$ is the $\gamma$ coordinate of the light ray at which the camera ray $(\alpha, \beta)$ is blocked.
**SVD Approximation**: Sample $\mathcal{I}(\beta, \gamma)$ on a $64 \times 64$ grid.
Compute the SVD of this sampled matrix on the CPU.
Select the top $N$ singular values and their corresponding left singular vectors $B_i(\beta)$ and right singular vectors $\Gamma_i(\gamma)$.
**Discretization and Visibility**: Approximate the inner integral as a Riemann sum.
Visibility $V(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ is 1 if the point is lit, 0 otherwise.
In epipolar coordinates, a point $(\alpha, \beta, \gamma)$ is lit if $\gamma < D(\alpha, \beta)$ and $S[\alpha, \gamma] > \beta$.
- Identify the lit segments along $\gamma$ where $S[\alpha, \gamma] > \beta$.
- Use 1D min-max mipmaps to accelerate finding these segments.
- Compute the sum over each segment using the precomputed prefix sum tables for $\Gamma_i(\gamma) \Delta \gamma$.
- Multiply by $B_i(\beta)$ and sum over $i=1 \dots N$.
- **Time Complexity**: Reduces computational cost from per-pixel to per-slice.
Instead of maintaining a partial sum tree for each $\beta$ (as in incremental integration), it computes only $N$ prefix sum tables per frame.
- **Memory Complexity**: Requires storage for the rectified shadow map, $N$ prefix sum tables, and the SVD components.
This method is part of the "Real-Time Volumetric Shadows using 1D Min-Max Mipmaps" technique, which uses epipolar coordinates and SVD to approximate multiple scattering in participating media.
